title: Korach: the staff that blossomed (Numbers 17:16–24)
hookLine: Aaron's staff sprouts blossoms and ripe almonds overnight

lines: AFTER THE GROUND, THE FIRE, THE PLAGUE.
cards: An almond tree in winter looks dead. Gray bark, bare branches, nothing. Then one week, while the cold is still hanging on, it's covered in white and pink blossom.

Hold that picture against the end of the Korach story. The ground has opened, fire has come down, and a plague has swept the camp. The people are terrified, and still muttering about who gets to serve.
God's final answer to the whole rebellion is not another disaster. It's a stick of dry wood, and what happens to it overnight.

teach.b: Here's the test, in paraphrase. Moses takes a staff from the leader of each of the twelve tribes and writes each leader's name on his staff. On the staff of the tribe of Levi he writes Aaron's name.
He lays all twelve in the Tent of Meeting overnight, and God says the staff of the one He chooses will sprout.
In the morning Moses goes in, and Aaron's staff, in the words of the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, had "put forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and bore ripe almonds."
Three seasons of a tree's year in one night: bud, flower and fruit, all on a dead stick. Moses brings out the staffs, and every leader takes his own back and looks at it. Only one has changed.

The Hebrew word for almond is shaked, and the prophet Jeremiah later makes a pun on it: he sees an almond branch, shaked, and God tells him He is shoked, watchful, over His word. So the almond is the wakeful tree.
And Aaron's staff isn't thrown away.
It's put back before the Ark and kept, as a sign for the rebellious, the text says, so that their complaints would end.

The argument about who serves is settled not by the loudest voice or the strongest punishment, but by something growing. After a rebellion that started with jealousy, the last word is a living thing nobody could fake.

how: The blossoming of Aaron's staff is read in synagogue as part of the portion of Korach, and later Jewish tradition counts the staff among the things kept beside the Ark.

games.q: the rebellion is over, but the people still mutter about who should serve as priest. how does the Torah settle it?
o: twelve staffs, left overnight in the tent.
games.why: twelve staffs overnight, and only Aaron's comes alive, with buds, blossoms and ripe almonds. the last word is something growing, not another punishment.

practice: Look out a window if there's one near you, or around the room, and find one living thing: a tree, a houseplant, a weed in a crack, even your own hand. Look at it as if it might change overnight.
Then turn inward: is something that looked dry for a long time, a friendship, a habit, a hope, starting just barely to come back?

wordCard.voice: Korach. A rebellion that ended with a flowering stick. And this week: forty years in the wilderness, the fringes, and five days with Korach, from a fair-sounding claim to an almond in bloom.

orig.note: Hebrew: almond, the fruit on Aaron's staff; Jeremiah plays it against shoked, watchful (Jeremiah 1:11–12).

carryVoice: Your line: the staff blossoms. Dry wood can still surprise you. That's day four hundred fifty-five.
